title: The weekend
goal: Master the rule that decides how your German sentences sound more than any other: the verb sits in second place, whatever comes before it.
bekal: put the verb in the right position
start a sentence with a time or place expression
say what you like doing with *gern*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Was machst du am Wochenende?
dialogs.intro: Friday afternoon. Watch the position of the verb in every sentence closely — some sentences start with the subject, some don't, but the verb never moves.

lines.speaker: Lena:
lines.id: What are you doing this weekend?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Am Samstag gehe ich ins Schwimmbad. Ich schwimme sehr gern.
lines.id: On Saturday I'm going to the pool. I love swimming.
lines.literal: on Saturday go I into-the swimming-pool. I swim very gladly.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ich gehe morgens um acht dorthin. Dann ist es noch leer.
lines.id: I go there at eight in the morning. It's still empty then.
lines.literal: I go mornings at eight there-to. then is it still empty.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Am Sonntag besuche ich meinen Onkel in Potsdam.
lines.id: On Sunday I'm visiting my uncle in Potsdam.
lines.literal: on Sunday visit I my uncle in Potsdam.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ja, ich fahre am Sonntag mit dem Zug nach Potsdam.
lines.id: Yes, I'm taking the train to Potsdam on Sunday.
lines.literal: yes, I ride on Sunday with the train to Potsdam.

lines.speaker: Lena:
lines.text: Das ist schön. Ich bleibe zu Hause und lese.
lines.id: That's nice. I'm staying home and reading.
lines.literal: that is beautiful. I stay at home and read.

lines.speaker: Lena:
lines.text: Sehr gern. Aber Sport mache ich nicht gern.
lines.id: Very much. But sports I don't like.
lines.literal: very gladly. but sport make I not gladly.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Vielleicht kommst du am Samstag mit?
lines.id: Maybe you'd like to come along on Saturday?
lines.literal: maybe come you on Saturday along?

lines.speaker: Lena:
lines.text: Um acht Uhr morgens? Nein danke!
lines.id: At eight in the morning? No thanks!
lines.literal: at eight o'clock mornings? no thanks!

notes: **Look at lines 2, 6, 8 and 12.** They all start with something other than the subject — *Am Samstag*, *Am Sonntag*, *Vielleicht* — and in all of them the subject steps behind the verb. What never moves is the verb itself: always the **second element** in the sentence.

**Compare lines 8 and 2 word by word.** *Ich fahre am Sonntag mit dem Zug nach Potsdam* and *Am Samstag gehe ich ins Schwimmbad*. The content can be arranged two ways, and both are correct. Whatever comes first is what you want to highlight.
***gern* is not a verb meaning "like".** It's an adverb that attaches to another verb: *Ich lese gern* = "I read gladly" = I like reading. The negative is *nicht gern*: *Ich koche nicht gern*.

**Line 11: *Sport mache ich nicht gern*.** Even the object of the action (*Sport*) can move to the front for emphasis — and the rule stays the same: verb second, subject third. To German ears this sounds completely natural; in English it only works in a few emphatic sentences ("Sports I don't like").
***mit dem Zug*, *mit dem Bus*, *mit dem Auto*** — means of transport always take *mit dem/der*. The exception is walking: *zu Fuß*. The form *dem* here is the Dativ, taken apart in Unit 13.
***zu Hause* and *nach Hause*.** The first means being at home (*Ich bleibe zu Hause*), the second means going home (*Ich gehe nach Hause*). Two frozen phrases to learn exactly as they are.

grammars.title: The verb in second place — the one rule
body: If you could remember only one rule of German grammar, this would be it. In a statement, **the conjugated verb is always the second element**. Not the second word — the second element: the block of meaning in front of it can be as long as you like.
after: ⚠️ The most typical English-speaker mistake: putting **two** elements in front of the verb — *Am Sonntag ich fahre nach Potsdam*, copying "On Sunday I'm going". That sentence instantly sounds foreign to a German, far more noticeable than a wrong article. If something moves to the front, the subject **must** step back.

This rule has two siblings you've been using since Unit 1: in **yes/no questions** the verb moves to **first** place (*Fährst du mit dem Zug?*), and in **commands** too (*Komm mit!*). A question word doesn't count as an ordinary first element — it simply belongs at the front, and the verb still follows it: *Wann **fährst** du?*

grammars.title: Order of expressions: time, manner, place
body: When a sentence contains more than one expression, their order isn't free. German arranges them **time → manner → place** — the reverse of the English habit, which puts place first.
after: Compare English: *I'm going **to Potsdam by train on Sunday*** — exactly backwards. Translating the English order word for word is one of the main sources of German sentences that are "correct but strange".

If one expression moves to first place, the rest stay in the same order: *Am Sonntag fahre ich mit dem Zug nach Potsdam.* The one that moves is usually the **time**, which is why everyday German sentences so often start with *heute*, *morgen*, *am Montag*.
The object of the action (Akkusativ) stands **before** the place expression but usually **after** the time expression: *Ich besuche **am Sonntag** meinen Onkel **in Potsdam**.*

blocks.text: Saying what you like and dislike

head: German
English
Note
rows: I'm not so keen on reading.

blocks.text: ⚠️ Don't say *Ich liebe lesen* to copy English *I love reading*. German uses *gern* for things you enjoy, and keeps *lieben* for love of people. You will hear *Ich liebe Pizza* in casual talk, but it sounds over the top — rather like declaring "I'm in love with pizza".
The fastest way to check your own sentence: point to the verb, then count backwards. If there's more than one element to its left, the sentence is wrong.

head: Wrong
Right
Why
rows: *Ich fahre nach Berlin mit dem Zug.*
Ich fahre **mit dem Zug nach Berlin**.

blocks.title: Five-minute drill
items: Take five sentences you've written in earlier units, and rewrite each with its time expression at the front.
Say both versions out loud, one after the other: *Ich gehe am Samstag ins Kino* / *Am Samstag gehe ich ins Kino*. Feel how the verb doesn't move.
If one of your versions sounds odd, check just one thing: how many elements come before the verb.
Am Samstag gehe ich ins Schwimmbad.
Ich fahre am Sonntag mit dem Zug nach Potsdam.
Ich bleibe zu Hause und lese.
